paras: The bombing of New Hope Baptist Church was a dynamite attack on a Black Baptist church at 19th Street and Waldron Avenue on the East Side of Kansas City, Missouri, on a Tuesday night in mid-May 1919, apparently May 13. The explosion damaged the church and nearby homes but injured no one reported, and no one was identified as the bomber. The Kansas City Sun called it "A DASTARDLY OUTRAGE" and tied it to threats against Black property, and its account was reprinted in the Metropolis Weekly Gazette and the Tulsa Star.

New Hope Baptist Church stood at 19th and Waldron and had a new pastor, S. W. Toles, who had come from seven years in Dallas, Texas, and added more than forty members in his first two months. In early May 1919 a letter in the Kansas City Sun from Mrs. J. R. Williams asked whether the city would answer Black demand for better housing "by resorting to threats of violence, by the use of dynamite." According to the Sun, an "element" had been "threatening for sometime on the East side to destroy Negro property."

On the Tuesday night before the Sun's issue of May 17, a charge of dynamite was exploded under the rear wall of the church. The blast seriously damaged the building and broke windows in several homes in the vicinity. A brick flat immediately south of the church, occupied by white people, suffered more than a hundred dollars in damage. The Sun's account mentions no one killed or injured. The Sun attributed the bombing "presumably" to "some miscreant" from the threatening element, but named no suspect.

Toles notified the police at once and insisted that protection be given to his property and congregation. He told the Sun that the church would be repaired immediately, a watchman installed, and services held as usual. The four or five Black families in the neighborhood said they were not frightened and would stay in homes "bought and paid for by hard labor."

A week later the church's column in the Sun reported Sunday services, a joint meeting with other congregations and the church's attendance at the District Board, without mentioning the explosion. No report of an investigation, arrest or prosecution was found.

The only first-hand account is the Kansas City Sun's front-page item of May 17, which drew on the pastor's own statement to "a representative of the Sun." The Metropolis Weekly Gazette reprinted it on its front page on May 23 without credit and without the closing paragraph on the Black families. The Tulsa Star ran the full text on May 24, credited to the "Kansas City (Mo.) Sun."

All three versions carried the headline "A DASTARDLY OUTRAGE" and presented the attack as part of a campaign against Black property, stressing the residents' refusal to be driven out. Weeks later The Plaindealer, addressing the mayor on Kansas City housing, complained that when Black buyers moved into white middle-class areas "then we hear of dynamite," and blamed the Kansas City Star for stirring sentiment.
The Sun and the Gazette placed the explosion on "last Tuesday night," while the Tulsa Star's reprint changed it to "Last Thursday Night"; the Sun's earlier local report is the better evidence.

bases: A charge of dynamite was exploded under the rear wall of a Black church, damaging property with no one reported hurt (A4).
Only the Kansas City Sun reported the explosion first-hand (A4); the Metropolis Weekly Gazette and Tulsa Star items are reprints of the same text (A6, A7), and no independent report was found.

accounts.label: Kansas City Sun local report
accounts.gist: Dynamite was exploded under the church's rear wall on 'last Tuesday night', presumably by someone from the element threatening Negro property on the East Side; the pastor and the Black families nearby vowed to stay.

accounts.label: Tulsa Star reprint
accounts.gist: The same text credited to the Kansas City (Mo.) Sun, with the day changed to 'Last Thursday Night'.

framing.detail: The Sun headlined it 'A DASTARDLY OUTRAGE', called the bomber a 'miscreant' and stressed the families' resolve to keep homes 'bought and paid for by hard labor'.
The Metropolis Weekly Gazette and the Tulsa Star reprinted the Sun's text and headline unchanged in tone.

conflicts.note: The Sun is the original local report and appeared first; the Tulsa Star text is a credited reprint, so its 'Thursday' is a copying change, not independent evidence. The Gazette and Star 'last' refer to the Sun's week, so May 20 (the Tuesday before the Gazette issue) is not supported.
